title: Postmortem & Action Plan for Streaming Termination Events after Capacity Surge
creator: Aisha Kapoor
description:
Summary:
On 2026-03-01 between 03:12-03:39 UTC a capacity surge across a subset of serving pools caused abrupt streaming terminations for ~0.9% of active streaming sessions. Symptoms reported by customers included disconnects mid-response and truncated token sequences (partial tokens). The incidents correlated with an autoscaler event that added and removed GPU nodes rapidly in a 20-minute window.

Observed impact:
- ~0.9% of streaming requests experienced disconnects or incomplete token sequences during the window.
- Affected tenants: 6 customers (mix of hosted and dedicated) with moderated user-visible errors (churned streams, client reconnects).
- No data loss beyond partial streamed outputs; KV caches persisted.

Initial mitigation implemented (03:20-04:00 UTC):
- Temporarily disabled aggressive node draining on the implicated autoscaler group to prevent mid-request interruption.
- Increased TCP keepalive and gRPC streaming timeouts on edge proxies to allow slow drains to finish.
- Rolled a conservative routing policy: prefer steady-state pools for long-lived streaming sessions.

Root cause analysis (summary):
We identified three compounding issues: (1) autoscaler oscillation: the horizontal autoscaler reacted to a transient CPU spike and performed scale-up followed by scale-down without sufficient cool-down, creating a short period of node churn; (2) request handoff race: the serving runtime did not reliably quiesce in-flight streaming connections before the node was terminated — the node drain sequence allowed the local proxy to close sockets early if KV cache flush/transfer took longer than the drain timeout; (3) backpressure amplification: when per-worker streaming buffers filled during the surge, the runtime opted to drop in-flight frames rather than apply controlled backpressure to upstream (edge) which resulted in truncated tokens being delivered.

Why regressions were possible now:
- A recent change (runtime PR #3124) shortened the node drain grace period to speed up restarts for a memory-leak patch. That change reduced headroom for finishing in-flight streaming requests in edge cases, which was acceptable under normal load but problematic during the surge.
- Monitoring did not have a composed alert that ties autoscaler churn, per-worker buffer occupancy, and gRPC server disconnect rate together, so the pattern wasn't a single alert prior to user reports.

Short-term fixes already completed (on-call):
- Reverted the reduced drain grace change for the affected pool (rolled back PR #3124 on 2026-03-01 04:05 UTC).
- Bumped default drain timeout for long-lived stream pools to 90s.
- Tuned edge & proxy keepalive and gRPC streaming timeouts to be more forgiving for slow drains.

Long-term action items (owners / ETA):
1) Robust drain protocol for streaming workers — implement handshake to ensure streams are drained or migrated before node termination. Owner: Marcus Lee. ETA: 2026-03-20. Estimate: 5 points.
2) Controlled backpressure path — change runtime to avoid dropping in-flight frames: implement backpressure signaling to proxies and graceful buffering fallback (spill-to-disk or stall) for sustained bursts. Owner: Priya Singh. ETA: 2026-04-10. Estimate: 8 points.
3) Autoscaler circuit-breaker — add hysteresis and a cooldown policy for pools that are serving long-lived streams; tie cooldown to active stream counts. Owner: Daniel Park. ETA: 2026-03-25. Estimate: 3 points.
4) Composite alerting and dashboard — create an observability rule that alerts on correlated signals (node churn rate, per-worker buffer > 80%, gRPC disconnect spike). Owner: Observability Team (Evan Morris). ETA: 2026-03-08. Estimate: 2 points.
5) Regression test harness — add load tests that simulate rapid bursts with long-lived streams to the CI gate for runtime changes affecting drain behavior. Owner: QA/Perf (Lina Chen). ETA: 2026-04-01. Estimate: 5 points.
6) Customer remediation playbook — write docs and automation to restart affected streams with session resume where possible. Owner: Solutions Eng (Marco Alvarez). ETA: 2026-03-15. Estimate: 2 points.

Acceptance criteria for each action (selected examples):
- Drain protocol: 99.9% of long-lived streams survive node termination when the pool has >50 active streams with no user-visible truncation in synthetic tests.
- Backpressure: runtime does not drop frames under a 2x burst; end-to-end latency under defined SLOs.
- Autoscaler: cooldown prevents >1 scale event per pool per 10 minutes under synthetic spikes.

Testing & rollout plan:
- Implement each change behind feature flags; run perf/stress tests in the staging cluster with controlled bursts and long-lived streams.
- Canary rollout to 10% of serving capacity in dedicated pools, monitor composite alert for 24 hours.
- Gradual ramp to 100% with circuit-breaker thresholds tuned during canary.

Monitoring / dashboards to add:
- Per-pool drain duration histogram and in-flight stream count during drain windows.
- Per-worker streaming buffer occupancy heatmap.
- Composite alert: node-churn > 3 in 10m AND gRPC disconnect rate > 0.5% AND buffer occupancy > 80% for 5m.

Open questions and trade-offs:
- Spill-to-disk for buffers reduces memory pressure but increases tail latency — acceptable for batch/embeddings but might impact conversational UX. Need UX/PM input.
- How aggressive should autoscaler hysteresis be before we harm our cost targets? Product input required.

Communication & customer follow-up:
- Notified affected customers on 2026-03-02 with incident summary and mitigation steps.
- Offer session-resume helper and priority support for tenants with critical SLAs.

Next steps (this ticket):
- Kickoff design doc for drain protocol, attach API sketch and sequence diagram. Owner: Marcus Lee. Due: 2026-03-05.
- Implement composite alert rule. Owner: Evan Morris. Due: 2026-03-08.
- Track dependent tickets ENG-8601 (autoscaler cooldown) and ENG-8619 (buffer metrics).

Postmortem note: This incident is primarily operational complexity compounded by a recent regression. The goal is to make streaming termination behavior deterministic and observable so small infra changes cannot cause user-visible truncation of generated output.
